Operators and sensors call AWS services, including Amazon SageMaker AI (training, processing, endpoints), AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, AWS Batch, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, AWS Lambda, Amazon ECS on Fargate, and Amazon EKS, as well as hundreds of community operators for other systems.
Automatic scaling of workers between a minimum and maximum you set; multiple schedulers for resilience.
Environment classes set the size of the scheduler and web server for the number of DAGs you run.
Access modes: the Airflow UI through a public endpoint on the internet or a private endpoint inside your VPC; in both cases access is controlled by IAM policies.
Move existing Airflow DAGs to AWS→ leads to Amazon MWAA
Airflow UI only inside the VPC→ leads to Private network access mode
Many parallel tasks at month end→ leads to Raise the maximum workers
Serverless, visual, AWS-native steps→ leads to Step Functions
SageMaker steps with model lineage→ leads to SageMaker Pipelines
Run one job every hour→ leads to EventBridge Scheduler
MWAA runs Apache Airflow for you: DAGs in S3, autoscaling workers, schedulers, and the web server in your VPC.
Choose it for existing Airflow skills and DAGs, and for Airflow's operators across AWS and other systems.
Secure it with an execution role, private subnets, KMS, Secrets Manager, and private access mode.
It is billed by the hour while the environment exists; Step Functions or SageMaker Pipelines can be cheaper for simpler or ML-only workflows.

Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) is a managed service for Apache Airflow, the open-source tool for creating, scheduling, and monitoring workflows written in Python. Each workflow is a DAG (directed acyclic graph) of tasks. You put DAGs in an Amazon S3 bucket, and MWAA runs the Airflow scheduler, workers that scale automatically, the web server, and the metadata database for you, inside a VPC, with AWS security built in.

Choose MWAA when a question describes existing Airflow DAGs, a team that knows Airflow, or pipelines that orchestrate many systems through Airflow operators and want the Airflow ecosystem, without running Airflow servers (MLA-C02 tasks 3.2.2 and 3.3).

The scheduler and workers run in private subnetsSubnetA range of IP addresses in a VPC, inside one Availability Zone. A subnet is public when its route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway, and private when it does not.Glossary entryClose of your VPC and use an execution role for AWS access; data and the environment are encrypted with KMS (AWS owned or customer managed keysCustomer managed keyA KMS key that you create, own, and manage: you control its key policy, rotation, and deletion. AWS managed keys, in contrast, are created and managed for you by an AWS service.Glossary entryClose); store connection secrets in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in DAG code. Private network access mode keeps the UI off the internet.
MWAA runs and patches Airflow; multiple schedulers and automatically scaled workers keep DAGs running; tasks can retry with backoff, and DAG code in versioned S3 can be rolled back.

Raise the maximum worker count for many parallel tasks, choose a larger environment class for more DAGs, and keep heavy processing in the services the tasks call (Glue, EMR, SageMaker AI) instead of on the workers.

You pay per hour for the environment (by class) plus additional workers and schedulers beyond those included, and metadata storage. An environment costs money while it exists, even when no DAG runs, so it suits frequent or complex orchestration. Amazon MWAA Serverless (since November 2025) is a deployment option with no environment to manage: each workflow runs with its own execution role and worker, and you pay for the compute time of the tasks that run. It uses Apache Airflow 3.

Airflow logs (scheduler, workers, tasks, web server) and environment metrics go to Amazon CloudWatch; the Airflow UI shows task history; CloudTrail records MWAA APIAPI (Application programming interface)A defined way for one program to ask another for data or actions, such as a set of HTTPS requests and responses. Every AWS service is controlled through its API, which the console, the CLI, and the SDKs call for you.Glossary entryClose calls.
